# Short answer

**No. If he had held his arm out forward (horizontally) instead of straight up above his head, the people nearest the camera would almost certainly not have thrown their hands in the air the way they do.** An arm held out forward is the *advantage* signal, which means "I've seen an infringement, but play carries on" — no whistle, ball still alive, nothing decided, so there is nothing to celebrate. The arm held **straight up above his head**, together with the whistle, is the opposite: it means play has been **stopped and a penalty awarded**, and here it goes **in favour of the light-blue team, Uruguay**, against the white-shirted side (Russia) who had the ball. Because it came on the very last play, that whistle ended the match — which is exactly why the crowd erupts.

---

# What is actually in the clip

**The setting.** This is rugby union: Uruguay (light-blue "celeste" jerseys with the *Antel* sponsor) versus Russia (white jerseys with red numbers), filmed handheld by a spectator from the stand. The hoardings on the far side read *Ovación*, *Antel*, *Volkswagen* and *RWC 2015* — this is the Rugby World Cup 2015 repechage second leg at the Estadio Charrúa in Montevideo, which Uruguay won 36–27 (57–49 on aggregate) to take the last place at the 2015 World Cup.

**"The guy in the orange" is the referee.** He is the only man on the field in the red-orange officials' shirt — you can read *Fly Emirates* across the chest at around 8.0 s and 10.4 s — with navy shorts and navy socks. He is a match official, not a player.

**What happens.** For the whole clip the white team (Russia) is hammering forward with a driving maul and successive close-range phases; at 9.2 s the ball is clearly visible in white hands inside the maul, so Russia are the team in possession and Uruguay are defending. The referee tracks alongside with his arms **down** throughout — he gives no signal at all while play is running. At roughly **10.4–10.5 s** the maul collapses into a heap of bodies on the ground, the referee blows his whistle (in several frames his other hand is up at his mouth on the whistle) and, while jogging in, **raises one arm straight up above his head with an open hand and holds it there** for close to two seconds (≈10.5 s to ≈12.3 s) before dropping it and walking in among the players.

**What the near-camera people do.** The instant the arm goes up, the spectator(s) directly in front of the lens fling **both hands up into the air above their heads** — first clenched fists, then open palms with the fingers spread, one wrist wearing a red band — waving them around and largely blocking the camera's view of the pitch. It is pure jubilation, in sync with the Uruguayan players on the field, who also throw both arms up, sink to the turf, and are mobbed by substitutes in green bibs running on.

---

# What his current arm position means

A single arm raised vertically and **held** aloft, accompanied by the whistle, is the referee's signal that **play has been stopped and a penalty awarded**. It is a terminal signal: the ball is dead, the decision is made, and the offending side gets nothing more. (Contrast the other one-armed signals — the free-kick signal is the arm *bent* at the elbow, and the advantage signal is the arm held *out from the body*; only the penalty is the full straight arm held up.)

**Which team it favours: Uruguay, the light-blue team.** A penalty always goes to the *non-offending* side, and here the arm goes up against the team in possession — Russia, who were the ones driving the ball forward when the maul went to ground. Every corroborating cue confirms the direction of the decision: the Uruguayan players celebrate instantly, the Russians stay slumped on the ground, and the Uruguayan bench empties onto the field.

**Why it ended the match.** The 80 minutes had already expired; past full time, play only continues until the ball next becomes dead. Awarding a penalty — an option to the non-offending team — makes the ball dead, so the referee's raised arm simultaneously killed Russia's final attack and ended the game. That is why the reaction isn't a mild "good, a penalty" but full-blown, match-winning celebration: Uruguay had just qualified for the World Cup.

---

# Why a forward arm would have produced a different reaction

**"Arm forward" is a different signal with the opposite meaning.** In rugby, an arm extended out from the body roughly horizontally, pointing in the direction the non-offending team is attacking, is the **advantage** signal. It means the referee has spotted an offence but is *not* stopping play — he is letting it run to see whether the non-offending side gets a territorial or tactical benefit first. Crucially, **no whistle is blown and the ball is still live**; he holds the arm out for several seconds and then either calls "advantage over" and play simply continues, or comes back and awards the penalty.

**So the crowd's hands would not have gone up.** The people in the foreground are reacting to *finality*, not to a refereeing opinion. With the arm held out forward:

- There is no whistle, so nothing signals the end of the passage, let alone the end of the match.
- Russia's attack would still be alive and going forward, with the clock already in the red — the most nerve-wracking possible moment for a home fan.
- The natural body language for that is the opposite of celebration: hands down, hands clamped over the mouth, gripping the rail, leaning in to watch the ball — at most tense, anticipatory gestures. Nobody throws both arms over their head while their team is still defending under pressure.

The hands-in-the-air only makes sense *after* an irreversible stoppage. That is precisely what the vertical arm delivers and what the horizontal arm explicitly withholds. Note also that the advantage signal would still be pointing *in Uruguay's favour* — so it is not the beneficiary that changes, it is whether the game has stopped.

**One caveat, which does not change the answer.** A roughly horizontal arm can also be used to award a **scrum**, pointing to the side that will feed, and after full time a scrum award would also have ended the game, so celebration would have followed eventually. But even then the reaction would not be the *same* or at the *same instant*: a scrum signal is a low-key restart signal that takes a crowd a beat to read, whereas the arm thrust straight up is unmistakable and produces the immediate explosion you see here. And in ordinary rugby usage "held his arm forward" means the advantage signal, under which play simply continues and the crowd's hands stay down.

Equally, if you read the raised arm purely as the referee's full-time gesture rather than as the penalty signal, the conclusion for the hypothetical is identical: an arm held forward means *play on*, and a crowd does not celebrate while the ball is still alive.
